advances:
The three-block collision geometry admits a global bound that charges excess fiber weight only to bins with at least one unit of remaining omitted slack in every block. A complete weighted antichain argument sharpens the local constant from 3/2 to the maximum of 1 and the sum of three explicit fractional-cost parameters. This gives a precise interface between the geometric capacity problem and two scalar weighted-geometric probability bounds.

The capacity conclusion below is conditional. The scalar probability bounds are not proved in this packet, and the unrestricted three-simplex capacity subgoal remains open unless those bounds, or another sufficient replacement, are established independently.

proof:
Pull back the barycentric coordinate functions of the three factors through an affine isomorphism and divide each by its positive value at \(\mathbf0\). This constructs the stated slacks and coefficients. The polytope is exactly the set where all slacks are nonnegative, and its interior is exactly the set where they are all positive. Each slack has constant term one. The maximal choices of the omitted coefficients give \(a_{b,i}\le1\), and the block relation gives \(1/\beta_{b,0}=1+\mu_b\).

For \(\mathbf I\in D\), define the selected bin coordinates and fractional parts by \(k_{b,i}(\mathbf I)=\lfloor f_{b,i}(\mathbf I)\rfloor\) and \(u_{b,i}(\mathbf I)=f_{b,i}(\mathbf I)-k_{b,i}(\mathbf I)\), where \(1\le i\le n_b\). Thus \(\mathbf k(\mathbf I)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^r\) and every \(u_{b,i}\in[0,1)\). For a bin \(\mathbf k\), let \(D_{\mathbf k}=\{\mathbf I\in D:\mathbf k(\mathbf I)=\mathbf k\}\), and define its discounted weight

\[
F_{\mathbf k}
=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D_{\mathbf k}}
2^{-\sum_{b=1}^3\sum_{i=1}^{n_b}u_{b,i}(\mathbf I)}.
\]

An empty fiber has weight zero. On a nonempty fiber, put \(\rho_b(\mathbf I)=\sum_{i=1}^{n_b}a_{b,i}u_{b,i}(\mathbf I)\). The block relation yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
f_{b,0}(\mathbf I)
&=C_b(\mathbf k)-\rho_b(\mathbf I),\\
C_b(\mathbf k)
&=\mu_b+1-\sum_{i=1}^{n_b}a_{b,i}k_{b,i},\\
0&\le\rho_b(\mathbf I)\le C_b(\mathbf k).
\end{aligned}
\]

Consequently a bin is empty if any \(C_b(\mathbf k)<0\).

For distinct \(\mathbf I,\mathbf J\in D_{\mathbf k}\), every selected slack difference lies strictly between \(-1\) and \(1\). Since the constant terms are one, all selected slacks are positive at both nonzero lattice vectors \(\mathbf I-\mathbf J\) and \(\mathbf J-\mathbf I\). Neither vector can be interior to \(P\). At least one omitted slack must therefore be nonpositive at each of these two vectors. Within the fixed bin, the omitted slack differences are the negatives of the \(\rho_b\)-differences. Thus there are two distinct block indices \(b,b'\) such that

\[
\rho_b(\mathbf I)-\rho_b(\mathbf J)\ge1,
\qquad
\rho_{b'}(\mathbf I)-\rho_{b'}(\mathbf J)\le-1.
\]

Equality is allowed in these two inequalities; it corresponds to a difference vector on a facet and is not excluded.

It follows that the vectors \(\mathbf j(\mathbf I)=(\lfloor\rho_1(\mathbf I)\rfloor,\lfloor\rho_2(\mathbf I)\rfloor,\lfloor\rho_3(\mathbf I)\rfloor)\) form an antichain in the coordinatewise order on \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^3\), and this map is injective on the fiber. Indeed, \(\mathbf j(\mathbf I)\le\mathbf j(\mathbf J)\) would imply \(\rho_b(\mathbf I)-\rho_b(\mathbf J)<1\) in every coordinate, contradicting the displayed positive gap.

We first give the elementary weight bound for such an antichain. A chain starting at \(\mathbf0\), at rank \(t\) and point \(\mathbf j\), increments coordinate \(b\) with probability \((j_b+1)/(t+3)\). It is uniform on each rank: induction gives, for \(|\mathbf j|=t\ge1\), probability \(t/((t+2)\binom{t+1}{2})=1/\binom{t+2}{2}\). Here \(|\mathbf j|=j_1+j_2+j_3\). The chain visits at most one point of a finite antichain \(A\), so

\[
\sum_{\mathbf j\in A}\frac1{\binom{|\mathbf j|+2}{2}}\le1,
\qquad
\sum_{\mathbf j\in A}2^{-|\mathbf j|}\le\frac32.
\]

For the second inequality, \(\binom{t+2}{2}2^{-t}\) has maximum \(3/2\), attained at \(t=1,2\): its ratio at consecutive ranks is \((t+3)/(2(t+1))\). Only the finitely many ranks meeting \(A\) are needed in the chain argument.

Since \(a_{b,i}\le1\), the total fractional sum at a point is at least \(\sum_b\rho_b\), and hence at least \(|\mathbf j|\). Applying the preceding inequality to the fiber antichain proves \(F_{\mathbf k}\le3/2\).

There is also a local bound of one whenever some \(C_b(\mathbf k)<1\). In that block the range of \(\rho_b\) is less than one, so it cannot supply either of the required unit gaps. The other two coordinates must therefore have opposite unit gaps for every pair. If the fiber has \(m\) points, list them in increasing order of one of these two coordinates. Its consecutive values increase by at least one, and the other coordinate's consecutive values decrease by at least one. Nonnegativity at the two ends shows that at position \(\ell\) these two coordinates are at least \(\ell-1\) and \(m-\ell\), respectively. The total fractional sum is thus at least \(m-1\) at every point, giving \(F_{\mathbf k}\le m2^{-(m-1)}\le1\). The last inequality follows from \(2^{m-1}\ge1+(m-1)=m\), and includes a singleton fiber.

For the sharper bound, observe that \(\sum_i u_{b,i}\ge\rho_b/c_b\). Therefore each fiber summand is at most \(\prod_{b=1}^3 q_b^{j_b}\). We will prove that every finite antichain \(A\subset\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^3\) satisfies

\[
\sum_{\mathbf j\in A}\prod_{b=1}^3q_b^{j_b}
\le\max\{1,Q\}
\qquad(0<q_b\le1/2).
\]

When \(Q\le1\), start a walk at \(\mathbf0\) which increments coordinate \(b\) with probability \(q_b\) and otherwise stops. The probability of reaching \(\mathbf j\) is \(\binom{|\mathbf j|}{j_1,j_2,j_3}\prod_bq_b^{j_b}\). The events of reaching different points of an antichain are disjoint, and the multinomial coefficient is at least one. Summing these probabilities proves the assertion. As before, stopping the construction after the largest rank in \(A\) suffices, including when \(Q=1\).

We supply a weighted rank argument for \(Q>1\). For \(d\in\{1,2,3\}\), write

\[
h_t^{(d)}
=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^d\\|\mathbf j|=t}}
\prod_{b=1}^d q_b^{j_b},
\qquad
\nu_t^{(d)}(\mathbf j)
=\frac{\prod_{b=1}^d q_b^{j_b}}{h_t^{(d)}}
\quad(|\mathbf j|=t).
\]

There is a chain whose distribution at rank \(t\) is \(\nu_t^{(3)}\). To prove this, construct couplings of each pair of consecutive rank laws, first for \(d=1\), then for \(d=2,3\), with the next point obtained by one coordinate increment. The one-coordinate case is immediate. The sequences \(h_t^{(1)}=q_1^t\) and \(h_t^{(2)}=\sum_{j=0}^t q_1^{t-j}q_2^j\) are log-concave in \(t\). For the second sequence the exact identity, valid for \(t\ge1\), is

\[
\bigl(h_t^{(2)}\bigr)^2-h_{t-1}^{(2)}h_{t+1}^{(2)}
=(q_1q_2)^t\ge0.
\]

This follows by expanding the finite geometric sums, also when \(q_1=q_2\). Thus the ratios \(h_{t+1}^{(d-1)}/h_t^{(d-1)}\) are nonincreasing for both induction steps.

At rank \(t\) in dimension \(d\), the last coordinate has probabilities \(p_t(j)=q_d^j h_{t-j}^{(d-1)}/h_t^{(d)}\), for \(0\le j\le t\). For \(0\le j\le t\),

\[
\frac{p_{t+1}(j)}{p_t(j)}
=\frac{h_t^{(d)}}{h_{t+1}^{(d)}}
\frac{h_{t+1-j}^{(d-1)}}{h_{t-j}^{(d-1)}}.
\]

This ratio is nondecreasing in \(j\), and the new distribution also has positive mass at \(t+1\). It follows that the rank-\(t+1\) last coordinate stochastically dominates the rank-\(t\) last coordinate. For completeness, across any cutoff, every likelihood ratio on the lower side is at most every ratio on the upper side; cross-multiplication of the two cumulative masses gives \(\sum_{j\le u}p_{t+1}(j)\le\sum_{j\le u}p_t(j)\).

In the other direction, \(p_{t+1}(j+1)=\alpha_t p_t(j)\), where \(\alpha_t=q_dh_t^{(d)}/h_{t+1}^{(d)}\in(0,1)\). The remaining mass is at zero. Hence the rank-\(t+1\) last coordinate is stochastically at most the rank-\(t\) last coordinate plus one. Using the same uniform variable in the two inverse cumulative distribution functions couples their values \(j,j'\) with \(j\le j'\le j+1\). If \(j'=j+1\), couple the other coordinates identically at rank \(t-j\). If \(j'=j\), use the already constructed consecutive-rank coupling in dimension \(d-1\). In each case the conditional marginals of the other coordinates are the required \(\nu_{t-j}^{(d-1)}\) and \(\nu_{t+1-j'}^{(d-1)}\). This constructs the desired coupling. Iterating its transition kernels constructs the rank chain through all ranks needed for the finite antichain.

The chain meets an antichain at most once, and therefore

\[
\sum_{\mathbf j\in A}
\frac{\prod_bq_b^{j_b}}{h_{|\mathbf j|}^{(3)}}\le1.
\]

We next show \(h_t^{(3)}\le Q\) for every \(t\ge0\) when \(1<Q\le3/2\). The case \(t=0\) is immediate. For the remaining ranks, consider the formal generating series \(H(z)=\prod_{b=1}^3(1-q_bz)^{-1}=\sum_{t\ge0}h_t^{(3)}z^t\). For distinct \(i,j\),

\[
(\partial_{q_i}-\partial_{q_j})H(z)
=\frac{(q_i-q_j)z^2 H(z)}{(1-q_i z)(1-q_j z)}.
\]

When \(q_i\ge q_j\), every coefficient on the right is nonnegative. Consequently moving weight from a smaller coordinate to a larger one, while keeping the sum fixed and each coordinate at most \(1/2\), cannot decrease any \(h_t^{(3)}\). After ordering the coordinates, perform such moves until two coordinates equal \(1/2\). This is possible because \(Q>1\); the third coordinate is then \(x=Q-1\in(0,1/2]\). It follows that

\[
h_t^{(3)}
\le \sum_{j=0}^t (t-j+1)2^{-(t-j)}x^j.
\]

For fixed \(t\ge1\), the right side is a convex polynomial in \(x\in[0,1/2]\). Its endpoint values are \((t+1)2^{-t}\le1\) and \(\binom{t+2}{2}2^{-t}\le3/2\). Bounding the polynomial by the chord between these endpoint bounds gives at most \(1+x=Q\). Combining this with the weighted rank inequality proves the claimed antichain bound, and therefore \(F_{\mathbf k}\le\max\{1,Q\}\).

The empty-bin criterion, the bound of one when some \(C_b<1\), and the last local bound together give the pointwise inequality

\[
F_{\mathbf k}
\le
\mathbf1_{\{C_b(\mathbf k)\ge0\ \text{for every }b\}}
+(Q-1)_+\mathbf1_{\{C_b(\mathbf k)\ge1\ \text{for every }b\}}.
\]

Using only the elementary local bound \(3/2\) gives the same inequality with \((Q-1)_+\) replaced by \(1/2\). Thus all possible excess above one is confined to bins with \(\sum_i a_{b,i}k_{b,i}\le\mu_b\) in every block. A bin with equality at either cutoff is included; no boundary bin has been discarded.

Affineness gives \(\boldsymbol\theta\cdot\mathbf I=(\log2)(r-\sum_{b,i}f_{b,i}(\mathbf I))\), where the sum is over the selected slacks. Regrouping by bins and then using the full independent geometric law yields the exact normalization

\[
\begin{aligned}
Z(\boldsymbol\theta)
&=2^r\sum_{\mathbf k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^r}
2^{-|\mathbf k|}F_{\mathbf k},\\
\frac{Z(\boldsymbol\theta)}{4^r}
&=\mathbb E F_{\mathbf K},
\qquad
\mathbb P(\mathbf K=\mathbf k)=2^{-r-|\mathbf k|}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The support \(D\) is finite, so the first sum has only finitely many nonzero terms. Taking expectations in the pointwise inequality and using independence of the three blocks proves the asserted global bound. Since \(Q\le3/2\), its second displayed upper bound follows as well. If \(Q\le1\), the excess coefficient vanishes. Each event \(Y_b\le\mu_b+1\) has probability strictly below one, because at least one positive coefficient multiplies an unbounded geometric variable. Thus \(Z(\boldsymbol\theta)<4^r\) in this case without any scalar hypothesis.

Finally assume the two scalar hypotheses with denominator 6, and suppose \(Q>1\). The first gives \(\prod_b\mathbb P(Y_b\le\mu_b)\le27/64\). The second and the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality give

\[
\frac{Z(\boldsymbol\theta)}{4^r}
\le\prod_{b=1}^3\left(1-\frac{q_b}{6}\right)
+(Q-1)\frac{27}{64}
\le\left(1-\frac{Q}{18}\right)^3
+(Q-1)\frac{27}{64}.
\]

The last expression is convex for \(Q\in[1,3/2]\), as its second derivative is \((1-Q/18)/54>0\). It is therefore at most its larger endpoint value. The endpoints are \((17/18)^3\) and

\[
\left(\frac{11}{12}\right)^3+\frac{27}{128}
=\frac{3391}{3456}<1.
\]

The second endpoint is larger: \((17/18)^3<17/18=3264/3456<3391/3456\). This proves the stated conditional quantitative bound. Together with the unconditional case \(Q\le1\), and \(B(P)\le Z(\boldsymbol\theta)\), it proves the conditional capacity conclusion.

If instead the scalar shifted-tail hypothesis has denominator 4, the shorter bound with excess coefficient \(1/2\) suffices for \(Q>1\):

\[
\frac{Z(\boldsymbol\theta)}{4^r}
\le\prod_{b=1}^3\left(1-\frac{q_b}{4}\right)+\frac{27}{128}
\le\left(1-\frac{Q}{12}\right)^3+\frac{27}{128}
\le\frac{3391}{3456}.
\]

The case \(Q\le1\) still follows from the elementary stopped-walk bound. This verifies both conditional consumers without supplying either unproved scalar hypothesis.

Every lattice operation in the geometric proof was subtraction in the original standard lattice. No factorwise lattice splitting or vertex-integrality assumption entered, and every point of the complete support, including every boundary point, contributed to its bin weight. No claim that the infimum defining \(B(P)\) is attained is needed for this reduction.
statement:
Let \(n_1,n_2,n_3\ge1\), put \(r=n_1+n_2+n_3\), and let \(P\subset\mathbb R^r\) be a full-dimensional polytope affinely isomorphic to a product of simplices of these dimensions. Suppose \(\operatorname{int}(P)\cap\mathbb Z^r=\{\mathbf0\}\). The vertices of \(P\) need not be lattice points. Retain the complete support \(D=P\cap\mathbb Z^r\), including its boundary points, and use the unnormalized capacity

\[
B(P)=\inf_{\boldsymbol\vartheta\in\mathbb R^r} Z(\boldsymbol\vartheta),
\qquad
Z(\boldsymbol\vartheta)=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}e^{\boldsymbol\vartheta\cdot\mathbf I}.
\]

For block \(b\in\{1,2,3\}\), let \(f_{b,0},\ldots,f_{b,n_b}\) be its affine facet slacks, normalized to equal one at \(\mathbf0\), and let \(\beta_{b,0},\ldots,\beta_{b,n_b}>0\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=0}^{n_b}\beta_{b,i}f_{b,i}=1\). These coefficients sum to one. Label a maximal coefficient in each block by \(0\). Define

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{b,i}&=\frac{\beta_{b,i}}{\beta_{b,0}}
\quad(1\le i\le n_b),
&\mu_b&=\sum_{i=1}^{n_b}a_{b,i},\\
c_b&=\max_{1\le i\le n_b}a_{b,i},
&q_b&=2^{-1/c_b},
&Q&=q_1+q_2+q_3.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(0<a_{b,i}\le1\), \(0<c_b\le1\), and \(0<q_b\le1/2\). Take the explicit tilt

\[
\boldsymbol\theta
=-(\log2)\sum_{b=1}^3\sum_{i=1}^{n_b}\nabla f_{b,i}.
\]

Let all \(K_{b,i}\) be independent with \(\mathbb P(K_{b,i}=m)=2^{-m-1}\) for \(m\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and put \(Y_b=\sum_{i=1}^{n_b}a_{b,i}K_{b,i}\). In particular, \(\mathbb E Y_b=\mu_b\). With \((Q-1)_+=\max\{Q-1,0\}\), the following unconditional bounds hold:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{Z(\boldsymbol\theta)}{4^r}
&\le
\prod_{b=1}^3\mathbb P(Y_b\le\mu_b+1)
+(Q-1)_+\prod_{b=1}^3\mathbb P(Y_b\le\mu_b)\\
&\le
\prod_{b=1}^3\mathbb P(Y_b\le\mu_b+1)
+\frac12\prod_{b=1}^3\mathbb P(Y_b\le\mu_b).
\end{aligned}
\]

In particular, \(Q\le1\) implies \(B(P)\le Z(\boldsymbol\theta)<4^r\).

Here is a precisely conditional consequence for the remaining coefficients. Suppose the following two probability inequalities hold for every integer \(m\ge1\), every \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in(0,1]\), and independent \(K_i\) with the preceding geometric law. Write \(Y=\sum_i a_iK_i\), \(\mu=\sum_i a_i\), and \(c=\max_i a_i\). The additional hypotheses are

\[
\mathbb P(Y\le\mu)\le\frac34,
\qquad
\mathbb P(Y>\mu+1)\ge\frac{2^{-1/c}}6.
\]

Under these hypotheses, every \(P\) above satisfies \(B(P)<4^r\); when \(Q>1\), the stated tilt satisfies the quantitative bound \(Z(\boldsymbol\theta)\le(3391/3456)4^r\). Replacing the denominator 6 in the scalar hypothesis by 4 also suffices, and then the elementary local constant 3/2 alone gives the same numerical conclusion. The scalar hypotheses are not assertions proved here. Their factor-specific versions for the three coefficient lists also suffice for the individual polytope.
